title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
summary: Create ConfigMaps and Secrets imperatively, feed them to Pods as env vars or files, and know what base64, immutability and encryption at rest really mean.

blocks.text: A ConfigMap holds **non-confidential** key-value data so you can keep environment-specific settings out of your container image. It gives you **no secrecy or encryption**; confidential values belong in a Secret.

items: Instead of `spec`, it has two optional fields: `data` (UTF-8 strings) and `binaryData` (base64-encoded binary). A key may not appear in both.
Keys may use alphanumerics, `-`, `_` and `.`. The object name must be a valid DNS subdomain name.
Size cap: **1 MiB**. For bigger config, mount a volume or use a separate service.
A Pod can only reference ConfigMaps in **its own namespace**.
A **static Pod** cannot reference a ConfigMap (or any other API object).

blocks.text: Four ways to use one in a Pod: in the container `command`/`args`, as environment variables, as files in a read-only volume, or by reading it through the Kubernetes API from your own code.

sections.heading: Create ConfigMaps imperatively
sections.sourceTitle: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

blocks.text:
kubectl create configmap <map-name> <data-source>

# literal values (repeat the flag for more keys)
kubectl create configmap <map-name> --from-literal=<key>=<value> --from-literal=<key2>=<value2>

# a file: key = file basename, value = file content
kubectl create configmap <map-name> --from-file=<path-to-file>

# a file under a key you choose
kubectl create configmap <map-name> --from-file=<my-key-name>=<path-to-file>

# every regular file in a directory
kubectl create configmap <map-name> --from-file=<directory>/

# an env-file of VAR=VAL lines
kubectl create configmap <map-name> --from-env-file=<path-to-env-file>

kubectl get configmap <map-name> -o yaml

items: From a directory, subdirectories, symlinks, devices and pipes are skipped, and files with invalid names can be missed **without an error**.
In an env-file, `#` comment lines and blank lines are ignored, and quotation marks are kept as part of the value.
Input that isn't ASCII or UTF-8 lands in `binaryData` instead of `data`.

blocks.text: Imperative is fastest: `kubectl create configmap <map-name> --from-literal=<key>=<value>`, then check it with `kubectl get configmap <map-name> -o yaml`. Keep `--from-file` and `--from-env-file` apart in your head: the first stores each **file** as one key, the second turns each **line** into a key.

sections.heading: Consume a ConfigMap in a Pod
sections.sourceTitle: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

blocks.text:
containers:
- name: <container>
  image: <image>
  env:                          # one key -> one variable
  - name: <ENV_NAME>
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: <map-name>
        key: <key>
        optional: true          # don't block startup if missing
  envFrom:                      # every key -> a variable of the same name
  - configMapRef:
      name: <map-name>
  volumeMounts:
  - name: config-volume
    mountPath: /etc/config
volumes:
- name: config-volume
  configMap:
    name: <map-name>
    items:                      # optional: only these keys, at these paths
    - key: <key>
      path: <file-name>

items: As a volume, each key becomes a file under `mountPath`. Files the image already had in that directory become inaccessible.
Use a ConfigMap-backed variable in `command`/`args` with the `$(VAR_NAME)` syntax.
A missing ConfigMap or key that is **not** marked optional stops the Pod from starting.
With `envFrom`, keys that aren't valid variable names are skipped. The Pod still starts, and an `InvalidVariableNames` event lists the skipped keys.

rows: Yes, eventually: up to the kubelet sync period plus its cache propagation delay

blocks.text: Set `immutable: true` (stable since v1.21) to lock a ConfigMap. This guards against accidental changes that cause outages, and cuts kube-apiserver load because watches on immutable ConfigMaps are closed.
Immutability is one-way. You cannot undo it or change `data`/`binaryData`; you can only delete and recreate the ConfigMap, and you should recreate the Pods that used it.

sections.heading: Secrets: types and the base64 trap

blocks.text: A Secret is like a ConfigMap but meant for small amounts of sensitive data such as passwords, tokens or keys. Values in `data` must be **base64-encoded**; that hides them from a casual glance but is **not encryption**. Use `stringData` to write plain strings; they are merged into `data`, and `stringData` wins if a key is in both. Each Secret is limited to **1MiB**.

rows: Default; arbitrary user data (`kubectl create secret generic`)
Certificate + key in `tls.crt` / `tls.key` (`kubectl create secret tls`)

blocks.text:
kubectl create secret tls <secret-name> --cert=<path/to/cert/file> --key=<path/to/key/file>
kubectl create secret docker-registry <secret-name> \
  --docker-server=<server> --docker-username=<user> \
  --docker-password=<password> --docker-email=<email>

By default Secrets sit **unencrypted in etcd**. Anyone with API or etcd access can read them, and so can anyone allowed to create a Pod (or a Deployment) in that namespace. Minimum hardening: enable **Encryption at Rest** for Secrets, use least-privilege RBAC, limit which containers get each Secret, and consider an external secret store.

sections.heading: Create and read a generic Secret

blocks.text:
# raw values: single-quote anything with $ \ * = or !
kubectl create secret generic <secret-name> \
    --from-literal=username=<user> \
    --from-literal=password='<password>'

# from files (key defaults to the file name; --from-file=<key>=<path> to rename)
echo -n '<user>' > ./username.txt
kubectl create secret generic <secret-name> --from-file=./username.txt

# read one value back
kubectl get secret <secret-name> -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode

items: `echo -n` matters: without it a trailing newline is written to the file and gets base64-encoded into the value.
`kubectl get` and `kubectl describe` don't print Secret contents by default; `describe` shows only byte counts.
`kubectl edit secrets <secret-name>` opens the base64 values for editing, unless the Secret is immutable.

blocks.text: Memorise `kubectl create secret generic <secret-name> --from-literal=<key>=<value>`, and to verify, pipe the jsonpath output through `base64 --decode`. Doing view and decode in one command also keeps the encoded value out of your shell history.

env:
- name: <ENV_NAME>
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: <secret-name>
      key: <key>
...
volumes:
- name: <volume-name>
  secret:
    secretName: <secret-name>
    optional: true

items: Secrets are **required by default**: no container starts until every non-optional Secret exists. A missing key in an existing Secret makes the Pod fail at startup.
Mounted Secrets are refreshed eventually (the kubelet's `configMapAndSecretChangeDetectionStrategy`, default Watch). `subPath` mounts are not refreshed.
`imagePullSecrets` (set at Pod level, or inherited from the ServiceAccount) lets the kubelet pull from a private registry.
A Secret goes only to nodes running a Pod that needs it, and the kubelet keeps it in **tmpfs**, never on durable storage.
Static Pods cannot use Secrets or ConfigMaps.
`immutable: true` works for Secrets as well, with the same one-way rule.
Any container with `privileged: true` can read every Secret used on its node.

flashcards.front: Which two data fields does a ConfigMap have, and what goes in each?
flashcards.back: data for UTF-8 strings; binaryData for base64-encoded binary. Keys can't overlap between them.

flashcards.front: Create a ConfigMap with two literal keys?

flashcards.back: The file's basename (unless you write --from-file=<my-key-name>=<path>). The value is the file content.

flashcards.front: Load every key of a ConfigMap as environment variables?
You update a ConfigMap. Do env vars in running Pods change?
flashcards.back: No. Env vars need a Pod restart. Volume mounts (not subPath) update eventually.

flashcards.front: How do you change an immutable ConfigMap?
flashcards.back: You can't. Delete and recreate it, then recreate the Pods that use it.

flashcards.front: Is base64 in a Secret's data field encryption?
flashcards.back: No. It only obscures the value; anyone who can read the Secret can decode it.

flashcards.front: Default Secret type, and the kubectl subcommand that creates it?
flashcards.back: Opaque, created with kubectl create secret generic.

flashcards.front: Which keys must a kubernetes.io/tls Secret have?
How are Secrets stored in etcd by default?
flashcards.back: Unencrypted. Enable Encryption at Rest to change that.

flashcards.front: Decode one key of a Secret in a single command?
Where does the kubelet keep Secret data mounted into Pods?
flashcards.back: In a tmpfs, so it isn't written to durable storage. It's deleted when the Pod goes.

questions.stem: Which command creates a ConfigMap named app-cfg with the key mode set to fast?

options.text: kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=mode=fast
options.explanation: --from-literal adds one key=value pair to data.

options.text: kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-env-file=mode=fast
options.explanation: --from-env-file expects the path of a file with VAR=VAL lines, not a literal.

options.text: kubectl create secret generic app-cfg --from-literal=mode=fast
options.explanation: That creates an Opaque Secret, not a ConfigMap.

options.text: kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-file=mode
options.explanation: --from-file reads a file or directory called mode; it doesn't set a literal value.

questions.stem: You run `kubectl create configmap web --from-file=nginx=./site.conf`. What key holds the content of site.conf?

options.text: nginx
options.explanation: The <my-key-name>=<path-to-file> form sets the key explicitly.

options.text: site.conf
options.explanation: The basename is used only when you don't give a key.

options.text: One key per line of site.conf
options.explanation: That's how --from-env-file behaves.

options.text: web
options.explanation: web is the ConfigMap's name, not a key.

questions.stem: A Pod reads LOG_LEVEL from a ConfigMap through env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef. You edit the ConfigMap. What happens to LOG_LEVEL in the running container?

options.text: Nothing; the Pod must be restarted to pick up the new value
options.explanation: ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables are not updated automatically.

options.text: It updates after the kubelet sync period plus cache delay
options.explanation: That's the behaviour for volume mounts, not env vars.

options.text: It updates immediately
options.explanation: Env vars are fixed when the container starts.

options.text: The kubelet restarts the container automatically
options.explanation: No automatic restart is described; you restart the Pod yourself.

questions.stem: Which of these keep a container from seeing later ConfigMap updates? Select 2.

options.text: Consuming the ConfigMap as environment variables
options.explanation: Env vars need a Pod restart.

options.text: Mounting the ConfigMap with a subPath volume mount
options.explanation: subPath mounts do not receive ConfigMap updates.

options.text: Mounting the whole ConfigMap as a volume
options.explanation: Full volume mounts are eventually updated by the kubelet.

options.text: Setting readOnly: true on the volumeMount
options.explanation: The docs recommend readOnly for ConfigMap mounts; it doesn't stop updates.

questions.stem: True or false: A Pod in namespace dev can mount a ConfigMap that lives in namespace prod.

options.text: True
options.explanation: The Pod and the ConfigMap must be in the same namespace.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Only code calling the API directly can read a ConfigMap in another namespace.

questions.stem: A ConfigMap has `immutable: true`. You need to change one value. What do you do?

options.text: Delete and recreate the ConfigMap, then recreate the Pods using it
options.explanation: Immutable data can't be changed; delete/recreate is the only path.

options.text: Set immutable: false, edit, then set it back
options.explanation: Marking a ConfigMap immutable cannot be reverted.

options.text: kubectl edit the data field
options.explanation: data and binaryData can't be mutated on an immutable ConfigMap.

options.text: Move the key into binaryData
options.explanation: binaryData is locked too.

questions.stem: A Pod uses envFrom with a ConfigMap that contains the keys 1badkey and LOG_LEVEL. What happens?

options.text: The Pod starts; 1badkey is skipped and an event records it
options.explanation: Invalid keys are skipped and listed in an InvalidVariableNames event.

options.text: The Pod fails to start
options.explanation: Invalid names don't block startup with envFrom.

options.text: The key is renamed to a valid name
options.explanation: No renaming happens; it's skipped.

options.text: kubectl rejects the Pod at creation
options.explanation: The Pod is admitted and allowed to start.

questions.stem: A ConfigMap volume is mounted at /etc/nginx/conf.d, and the image already ships files in that directory. What happens to those image files?

options.text: They become inaccessible; only the ConfigMap's files are visible
options.explanation: The docs warn that existing files in the mount directory become inaccessible.

options.text: They are merged with the ConfigMap's files
options.explanation: The mount hides what was there.

options.text: They are copied into the ConfigMap
options.explanation: Nothing is copied back into the ConfigMap.

options.text: The Pod fails to start
options.explanation: The Pod starts normally.

questions.stem: True or false: Because Secret values are base64-encoded, they are encrypted.

options.text: True
options.explanation: base64 obscures a value but is not secret; anyone who can read it can decode it.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd unless you enable Encryption at Rest.

questions.stem: Which steps does the Secrets page list as the minimum for using Secrets safely? Select 3.

options.text: Enable Encryption at Rest for Secrets
options.explanation: Listed first.

options.text: Configure least-privilege RBAC access to Secrets
options.explanation: Listed.

options.text: Restrict Secret access to specific containers
options.explanation: Listed.

options.text: Store values in stringData instead of data
options.explanation: stringData is just a write convenience; values end up in data either way.

questions.stem: A Secret manifest sets the key password in both data and stringData. Which value is stored?

options.text: The stringData value
options.explanation: stringData is merged into data and takes precedence.

options.text: The data value
options.explanation: stringData wins when a key appears in both.

options.text: The API server rejects the Secret
options.explanation: Both fields are allowed together.

options.text: Both values, concatenated
options.explanation: Values are not concatenated.

questions.stem: You need a Secret holding a certificate and private key for an Ingress. Which command fits?

options.text: kubectl create secret tls <secret-name> --cert=<cert-file> --key=<key-file>
options.explanation: Creates a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with tls.crt and tls.key.

options.text: kubectl create secret docker-registry <secret-name> --docker-server=<server>
options.explanation: That makes a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret for registry auth.

options.text: kubectl create configmap <name> --from-file=<cert-file>
options.explanation: ConfigMaps aren't meant for confidential data like private keys.

options.text: kubectl create secret generic <secret-name>
options.explanation: generic creates an Opaque Secret (here an empty one), not a kubernetes.io/tls Secret.

questions.stem: You created a Secret from a file written with plain `echo '<password>' > pw.txt`, and the app's login keeps failing. What's the likely cause?

options.text: A trailing newline was written to the file and encoded into the value; use echo -n
options.explanation: The -n flag prevents the extra newline that otherwise ends up in the base64 value.

options.text: Files can't be used with kubectl create secret generic
options.explanation: --from-file is a documented way to create a generic Secret.

options.text: The value needs to be base64-encoded before writing it to the file
options.explanation: kubectl does the encoding itself when it reads the file.

options.text: Secrets created from files are type kubernetes.io/basic-auth
options.explanation: generic creates an Opaque Secret.

questions.stem: A Pod mounts a Secret volume (not marked optional), and the Secret doesn't exist yet. What happens?

options.text: No container starts; the kubelet keeps retrying and records an Event
options.explanation: Secrets are required by default, and the kubelet retries periodically and reports an Event.

options.text: The containers start with an empty mount
options.explanation: Only an optional Secret that is missing gets ignored; a required one blocks every container.

options.text: The kubelet creates an empty Secret
options.explanation: The kubelet never creates the Secret.

options.text: The Pod is rescheduled to another node
options.explanation: Rescheduling doesn't help a missing Secret, and isn't described.

questions.explanation: Secrets are deleted like any other object: `kubectl delete secret <name>`.
